ambiguities: How much of the account should a single position be allowed to use at most — a small fixed slice (e.g. 5% per position, many small bets), a medium slice (e.g. 20%, a handful of positions), or let it concentrate into one big bet? This changes how many trades the lab makes and how much any one loss hurts.

What should the daily-loss halt be — stop trading for the day after losing a small amount (e.g. 1% of the account), a medium amount (e.g. 3%), or a larger amount (e.g. 5%)? A tighter halt stops bleeding sooner but may cut off a recovery.

How many orders per day should the lab be allowed to send at most — a low cap (a few trades), a medium cap (a dozen or so), or a high cap (many trades)? More trades means more chances but also more fees and noise.
Which instruments should be on the allow-list — only large, liquid stocks and broad ETFs (safest, easiest to trade), or also smaller or more volatile stocks (more opportunity, more risk)?
How often should the lab propose trades — continuously as signals arrive, once a day at a set time, or only when the operator asks it to look? This sets how hands-on the operator has to be.

When the lab proposes a trade, should the operator approve each one individually, approve a batch at once, or set standing rules that auto-approve within limits? Individual approval is safest but more work; standing rules are less work but less oversight.

What should the operator view show most prominently — just the account vs SPY over time, or also the list of recent proposals, approvals, and fills with their rationales? This decides what the dashboard is built around.

How should the lab decide which public signals matter most — weigh insider filings (Form 4/13F) heaviest, weigh news and Reddit heaviest, or treat them all roughly equally? This shapes what the research step actually looks for.
user_feedback: Operator answers to the brief's questions: (1) one position may use at most 5% of the paper account; (2) halt trading for the day after a 3% daily loss; (3) at most about 3 orders a day, on an allow-list of large, liquid US stocks and broad ETFs only; (4) the operator approves each order individually; (5) the lab proposes once a day at a set time before the market opens; (6) the operator view shows both the account against SPY over time and the recent proposals, approvals and fills with their rationales; (7) weigh SEC Form 4 insider purchases heaviest, then 13F and Congressional disclosures, with news and Reddit as context. Plan only -- nothing is executed until the operator says so.
